blocks.text: 1. Embedding Fine-Tuning

blocks.alt: A pretrained embedding model goes through fine-tuning to become domain-adapted

blocks.text: Embedding Fine-Tuning moves from choosing a model to customizing one, adapting a pretrained embedding model to a specific domain.
It continues training an already existing embedding model on domain specific examples.
2. Starting From A Pretrained Model
As with the general purpose versus domain specific tradeoff in Embedding Models, a general purpose model already understands broad language well.
Fine tuning starts from that strong foundation rather than training from scratch.
3. Why General Models Fall Short

blocks.alt: A general model is compared against domain-specific jargon

blocks.text: Specialized vocabulary and domain specific relationships are not always well represented in general training data.
As with the general purpose versus domain specific distinction in Embedding Models, a legal or medical term can mean something narrower than its everyday sense.
4. Building Training Pairs

blocks.alt: A query and its relevant document form a positive pair

blocks.text: Fine tuning needs examples of which text pairs should be considered similar or dissimilar.
Real query and relevant chunk pairs make excellent training examples for this purpose.

blocks.text: 5. Contrastive Training Objective

blocks.alt: A positive pair is pulled closer while a negative pair is pushed farther

blocks.text: As with similar meaning means nearby points in What are Embeddings, training pulls similar pairs closer and pushes dissimilar pairs apart.
This repeats over many examples until the model's own vector space reflects the domain.
6. How Much Data Is Needed
Fine tuning requires far less data than training an embedding model from scratch.
Even a modest set of well chosen domain examples can meaningfully shift the model's behavior.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: A few thousand carefully chosen query and chunk pairs can produce a meaningfully improved domain specific model, in sharp contrast to the millions of examples needed to train an embedding model from nothing.

blocks.text: 7. Risk Of Over Tuning

blocks.alt: An over-tuned model loses its general ability

blocks.text: Fine tuning too aggressively on a narrow dataset can degrade the model's broader general understanding.
A careful balance keeps domain gains without losing general capability entirely.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: A model fine tuned too heavily on a narrow set of examples can start performing worse on queries that fall even slightly outside that narrow training distribution, a real risk that needs careful monitoring.

blocks.text: 8. Evaluating The Fine-Tuned Model

blocks.alt: A fine-tuned model is compared against the original model

blocks.text: As with benchmarking embedding models in Embedding Models, comparing retrieval quality before and after fine tuning reveals whether it actually helped.
A dedicated evaluation step, the subject of the next topic in this module, confirms real improvement.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Embedding Fine Tuning Is Worth The Effort

blocks.alt: Highly domain-specific vocabulary points toward fine-tuning the embedding model

blocks.text: A narrow, specialized domain with distinctive vocabulary benefits most.
Broad, general purpose content often performs well with an off the shelf model already.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Fine tuning from scratch instead of starting from a strong pretrained general purpose model.
Using too narrow or too small a set of training pairs, risking overfitting to specific examples.
Fine tuning so aggressively that the model loses its broader general understanding entirely.
Skipping evaluation and assuming fine tuning helped without measuring retrieval quality before and after.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Embedding fine tuning continues training an already existing model on domain specific examples.
It starts from a strong pretrained foundation rather than training an embedding model from scratch.
General models can fall short on specialized vocabulary not well represented in broad training data.
Real query and relevant chunk pairs make excellent training examples for fine tuning.
A contrastive objective pulls similar pairs closer together and pushes dissimilar pairs apart.
Fine tuning requires far less data than training an embedding model from scratch.
Over tuning on a narrow dataset can degrade a model's broader general understanding.
Comparing retrieval quality before and after fine tuning confirms whether it actually helped.
